title: Fold a list of rules with and() and or()

blocks.text: `p1.and(p2)` short-circuits like `&&`: if `p1` says `false`, `p2` is never asked. `p1.or(p2)` short-circuits like `||`. Both refuse a `null` argument with a `NullPointerException` right where they are called.

items: `allOf(List<Predicate<T>> rules)` returns a predicate that is true when every rule is true; `and()` is the page's tool.
`anyOf(List<Predicate<T>> rules)` returns a predicate that is true when at least one rule is true; `or()` is the page's tool.

blocks.text: A list may be empty, and rules may be expensive: each rule is asked at most once per `test`. A list holding `null`, even a list holding nothing but `null`, is a caller's bug: report it as early as `and()` and `or()` themselves would. The predicate is fixed when it is built: changing the list afterwards does not change it.

cases.says: allOf passes when every rule passes; anyOf passes when at least one does.
With no rules, allOf accepts everything and anyOf accepts nothing.
Like && and ||, a rule is not run once the answer is already decided.
A null rule makes building the predicate throw NullPointerException at once, not later at test time.
The predicate is fixed when it is built: adding a rule to the list afterwards changes nothing.
A list holding only null is rejected when building too.
A test of the combined predicate asks each rule at most once.

origin.section: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

concepts: and() and or() reject a null predicate when they are called, not later when the result is tested.
Always-true and always-false predicates are the neutral starting points for and() and or().
and() and or() short-circuit like && and ||, so a later predicate may never run.
